title: The river and the fish
hookLine: You are the river, all-knowing; I am a fish, how can I find Your end (Sri Rag M1, ang 25)
tomorrow: The four watches of the night

lines: DOES A FISH KNOW IT'S WET?
IT CAN'T STEP BACK AND SEE.
cards: Here's an old riddle: does a fish know it's wet? It has never been anywhere else. Water is above it, below it, inside its gills, carrying its food, holding up its weight.
The one thing a fish can't do is step back and see the water. Guru Nanak, from the land of five rivers, wrote a hymn that swims close to that riddle. In it he doesn't play the river.

teach.h: YOU ARE THE RIVER; I AM A FISH.
teach.b: The shabad is in Sri Rag, on ang 25. It begins, in effect: You are the river, all-wise, all-seeing; I am a little fish, how could I ever find Your end? The word for the fish is machhuli, a small fish, almost affectionate.
Then the refrain: wherever I look, there You are; pulled out of You, I burst and die.
That's the hymn in one picture. The fish can't measure the river or get outside it to see where it starts or ends. It doesn't need to.
It just needs to stay in it. Out of the water, a fish doesn't become free. It suffocates.
Then a very honest line. I don't know the fisherman, Guru Nanak says, and I don't know the net.

teach.h: I CALL ON YOU WHEN PAIN COMES.
teach.b: But when pain comes, then I call on You. He admits what a lot of people would rather not: that we often remember the river only when we're flapping on the bank.
And then a correction: You are present everywhere; I thought You were far away. Whatever I do is done in Your presence. Here's the gentle thing.
Elsewhere Gurbani talks about separation from God as a kind of exile. This shabad suggests the separation is partly an illusion.
The fish thinks the river is somewhere else because it's never seen it from outside, but it has never once been outside it.
For Sikhs, that's what naam, remembering the Name, does: not bringing God close, but noticing how close God has been all along.

how: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its refrain, wherever I look, there You are, is often repeated by the congregation.

o: the river that holds all the fish
the fisherman who casts the net there
a little fish, the singer before the river

games.q: the river and the fish — tap the pairs.

s: in this hymn Guru Nanak speaks as the river
he speaks as the fish; the One is the river.
the hymn admits we often remember God only in pain
I don't know the fisherman or the net, but when pain comes, I call on You.
the hymn says God is far away
I thought You were far; You are present everywhere.

games.q: you're a little fish who wants to find where the river ends. what does Guru Nanak's fish conclude?
o: swim until you find the end.
you can't find its end, and you don't need to.
jump out to see it from above.
games.why: how could I ever find Your end? and out of You, I'd die. the fish's life is in the river.

practice: Watch water move: run a tap slowly, pour from one glass into another, or look at rain or a fountain, and if none is near, picture one clearly.
See how it moves without effort and fills whatever shape it's given, then notice what surrounds you right now: air, light, the ground holding you up, all of it unasked for.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru, a fish thanking the river.

wordCard.voice: Machhuli, a little fish: Guru Nanak says, You are the river, I am a machhuli; wherever I look, You are there, and out of You I die.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a little fish; the small creature Guru Nanak becomes in this hymn.

carryVoice: Your line: a fish in the river. In the hymn, the river was never far. That's six hundred forty-nine.

sources.ref: Sri Rag M1, Ang 25 (tu dariaao daanaa beenaa)
